sections.title: Technique & Approach
sections.content:
## RFA Technique Essentials

Radiofrequency ablation uses thermal energy to create a lesion that interrupts the medial branch nerve, preventing pain signal transmission from the facet joint.

### Step-by-Step Procedure

1. **Patient positioning**: Prone on fluoroscopy table
2. **Level identification**: AP fluoroscopy to identify target transverse processes at each level
3. **Electrode placement**: The RF electrode (typically 18-22 gauge cannula with active tip) must be placed **PARALLEL to the medial branch nerve** along the junction of the transverse process and SAP
4. **Why parallel matters**: Standard thermal RFA creates a lesion approximately 1 cm long by the width of the electrode shaft. Parallel placement **maximizes contact** between electrode and nerve. Perpendicular placement may miss the nerve entirely.
5. **Confirm position**: AP and lateral fluoroscopy
6. **Sensory stimulation**: At **50 Hz** — concordant pain reproduction at <0.5 V suggests optimal placement near the target nerve
7. **Motor stimulation**: At **2 Hz** — should see multifidus muscle contraction (confirming medial branch proximity) and **absence of limb motor response at <2.0 V** (confirming the electrode is not near a motor nerve root)
8. **Local anesthetic**: Inject **0.5-1 mL** of local anesthetic before each lesion to reduce procedural pain
9. **Lesion creation**: Heat to **80-85 degrees C for 60-90 seconds** per lesion
10. **Multiple lesions**: Consider creating **2-3 overlapping lesions per level** to increase the probability of capturing the nerve

### Lesion Parameters

| Parameter | Standard Value |
|-----------|---------------|
| Temperature | 80-85 degrees C |
| Duration | 60-90 seconds |
| Sensory stimulation | 50 Hz, <0.5 V |
| Motor stimulation | 2 Hz, no limb response at <2.0 V |
| Lesion size | ~1 cm long x electrode diameter |

### IPSIS Cervical RFN Technique Details

The IPSIS evidence-based technique for cervical medial branch radiofrequency neurotomy (CMBRFN) has specific hallmarks:

#### Cannula and Electrode Selection
- **Large-gauge cannulae (16G or 18G)** with a 10 mm sharp, bent active tip are preferred
- Available in 100 mm and 145 mm lengths
- The RF cannula bevel direction is **non-coincident** with the hub notch (opposite of spinal needles) — the cannula deflects toward the hub notch/dot marking
- Recent consensus guidelines have advised safety studies before using alternative technologies (bipolar, cooled RF, multi-tined) in the cervical spine

#### Cervical Target Zones
- Because medial branches assume **variable positions** relative to their articular pillars, there is no single electrode placement point — instead, there is a **zone of likely nerve location** that must be covered
- **Typical levels (C3-6)**: The C5 medial branch is consistently at the mid-pillar; C3, C4, and C6 branches are progressively higher. Two parallel large-gauge cannula placements in the middle and upper aspects of the lateral pillar are typically needed
- **C5 level**: May only need one cannula placement if using 16G
- **C7 medial branch**: Three lesion locations needed (C7 SAP apex, SAP base, and root of the transverse process). The narrow C7 SAP requires a near-sagittal or slightly (5 degrees) ipsilateral oblique trajectory to avoid passing into the C6-7 neural foramen
- **Third occipital nerve (TON)**: Three lesion locations along the C2-3 joint (equator, cephalad, caudal to joint)

#### Critical Safety — Depth Control
- The **cannula tip must NEVER advance ventral to the anterior margin of the articular pillar** (C3-6) or the SAP (C7/TON)
- **Foraminal oblique views** provide essential auxiliary imaging to verify the cannula is safely posterior to the cervical foramen and exiting nerve/vertebral artery
- If the physician is uncertain about cannula position relative to vulnerable structures, **RF lesioning should NOT commence**

#### Cervical Lesion Parameters
- Temperature: **80-85 degrees C for at least 90 seconds** per lesion
- Multiple tightly overlapping lesions are made to cover the entire zone of nerve probability
- The cannula must be manually held in place during lesioning if it is mobile

### IPSIS Lumbar RFN Technique Details

#### Cannula Trajectory and Placement
- **15-20 degrees ipsilateral obliquity** helps avoid the mamillo-accessory ligament (MAL) when positioning the cannula alongside the nerve
- Excessive obliquity (25-30 degrees) results in a more transverse approach that is less parallel to the nerve and less effective
- A **declined fluoroscopic tilt of approximately 35-40 degrees** is required to parallel the nerve as it crosses the lateral SAP base
- True lateral imaging establishes cannula depth: the active tip should overlie the **middle two-fourths** of the lateral SAP for L1-4 medial branches
- For the L5 dorsal ramus, the cannula should be over the **posterior two-thirds** of the S1 SAP

#### Avoiding Collateral Nerve Injury
- Do NOT lesion over the **ventral one-fourth of the SAP** (L1-4) or **ventral one-third of the S1 SAP** (L5 DR) to avoid lateral/intermediate branch injury
- Do NOT lesion over the **posterior one-fourth of the SAP** (L1-4) where the nerve may escape beneath the MAL
- This MAL concern does not apply to the L5 DR target (MAL is rudimentary/absent at S1)

#### Lumbar Lesion Parameters
- Temperature: **80-85 degrees C for 90 seconds**
- A properly placed single 16G cannula should cover all possible medial branch locations at a given level
- If using 18G or smaller, additional placements and lesions are needed to create an equivalent lesion zone
- For the L5 DR, the deep sulcus means a second higher lesion placement is usually unnecessary; instead, the cannula can be withdrawn 3-5 mm to extend the lesion length

### Advanced Technology: Cooled RF

Cooled radiofrequency is a newer technology that internally cools the electrode tip during lesioning:
- Creates **larger, more spherical lesions** compared to conventional RF
- May **improve nerve capture rates**, especially for anatomically variable nerves
- Particularly useful for SI joint lateral branch ablation where nerve courses are variable
- Most positive SI joint RFA studies use cooled RF technology

### Post-Procedure Expectations

- **Onset of relief**: May take **2-6 weeks** due to Wallerian degeneration of the nerve
- **Temporary neuritis**: ~5% of patients experience temporary worsening of pain for 1-4 weeks as the nerve degenerates
- **Full effect**: Typically achieved by 6-8 weeks post-procedure
- Patients should be counseled about the delayed onset to prevent premature conclusions of failure
keyPoints: Electrode MUST be placed parallel to the medial branch nerve to maximize lesion-nerve contact
Standard lesion: 80-85 degrees C for 60-90 seconds creates a ~1 cm lesion
Sensory stimulation at 50 Hz (<0.5 V) confirms proximity; motor at 2 Hz confirms no motor nerve root involvement
Consider 2-3 overlapping lesions per level to increase nerve capture probability
Relief onset is delayed 2-6 weeks due to Wallerian degeneration — counsel patients accordingly
Temporary post-procedure neuritis occurs in ~5% of patients
Cooled RF creates larger lesions and may improve capture rates for variable nerve anatomy
IPSIS hallmarks: rigorous patient selection, accurate anatomic views, parallel cannula placement, large-gauge (16-18G) cannulae, multiple lesions
Cervical: target a ZONE of nerve probability, not a single point — variable nerve positions require multiple lesion placements (IPSIS)
Cervical safety: cannula tip must NEVER advance beyond the anterior margin of the articular pillar; use foraminal oblique views to confirm (IPSIS)
Lumbar: 15-20 degrees ipsilateral obliquity + 35-40 degrees declination parallels the cannula to the nerve at the SAP base (IPSIS)
Lumbar lesion zone: middle two-fourths of SAP for L1-4; posterior two-thirds of S1 SAP for L5 DR — avoid ventral and posterior extremes (IPSIS)
If uncertain about cannula position relative to vulnerable structures, do NOT commence RF lesioning (IPSIS)

sections.title: Clinical Decision-Making
sections.content:
## Patient Selection — The Most Critical Factor

Patient selection is **THE most critical determinant** of RFA success. The rigor of the diagnostic block criteria directly predicts outcomes.

### Selection Criteria

- **Minimum relief threshold**: >80% pain relief on **dual (controlled) medial branch blocks** is the standard criterion
- **Concordant pain response**: Duration of relief must match the pharmacology of the anesthetic used
- **Appropriate pain pattern**: Predominantly **axial pain** without significant radicular component
- **Failed conservative care**: Documentation of failed PT, medications, and other conservative measures
- **Imaging consideration**: While not required, evidence of facet arthropathy on imaging supports the diagnosis

### The 80% vs 50% Relief Threshold Debate

This is an important clinical and insurance issue:
- Studies using the **>80% threshold** show significantly better RFA outcomes
- Studies using **>50% threshold** show worse outcomes and contributed to controversial negative trials
- **Cohen SP et al. (2010)**: Demonstrated that outcomes are directly related to the rigor of diagnostic block criteria
- **Best practice**: Use >80% as the threshold for proceeding to RFA

### The Juch MINT Trial Controversy (2017)

The JAMA MINT trial by Juch et al. found no significant difference between RFA + exercise vs exercise alone. This trial was **heavily criticized** for methodological issues:

1. **Single blocks only** — not controlled dual blocks
2. **50% relief threshold** — too low for proper patient selection
3. **Short follow-up (3 months)** — inadequate because RFA typically takes 4-6 weeks for full effect
4. **Technical concerns** about electrode placement
5. **Included patients who may not have had true facet-mediated pain**

This trial illustrates why patient selection methodology matters enormously for RFA outcomes.

### Repeat RFA Considerations

- **Nerve regeneration**: Medial branch nerves regenerate typically within 6-18 months
- **Timing**: Repeat when pain recurs after a previously successful procedure (usually 9-18 months)
- **Success of repeat**: ~80% of patients who responded to the first RFA will respond to repeat procedures
- **Insurance**: Most payers cover repeat RFA when the initial was successful; some require interval diagnostic blocks

### When NOT to Pursue RFA

- Failed controlled diagnostic blocks (<80% relief)
- Predominantly radicular symptoms
- Young patients (<35) without clear imaging-confirmed facet arthropathy
- Untreated psychological comorbidities (catastrophizing, secondary gain)
- Inability to participate in post-procedure rehabilitation

### Pre-Procedure Imaging for RFN (IPSIS)

- Pre-procedure MRI or CT is indicated to screen for acquired, degenerative, or congenital anatomic derangements that would make the procedure unsafe or unlikely to succeed
- In the cervical spine, imaging can identify aberrant vertebral artery loops near the C2-3 targets and assess articular pillar morphology
- In the lumbar spine, cross-sectional and sagittal imaging help plan cannula trajectory and identify the SAP/TP junction anatomy
- However, imaging findings are NOT diagnostic for facet pain — patient selection is based on response to controlled MBBs, not imaging

### Special Populations (IPSIS)

#### Patients with Cardiac Implantable Devices
- No known reports of RFN causing PPM/ICD dysfunction leading to serious injury, but caution is warranted
- Highest risk: pacemaker-dependent patients, patients with ICDs, and RFN planned at L3 or above
- Risk mitigation: contact the cardiologist/electrophysiologist, use continuous ECG monitoring, place dispersive pad >15 cm from pacing leads
- A magnet over the device may be used to inhibit triggering if recommended by the cardiologist
- Bipolar RFN techniques reduce the risk of interference with cardiac devices

#### Patients with Fusion Hardware
- Posterolateral fusions destroy the medial branch at fused levels through surgical exposure
- Only the medial branch at the unfused adjacent level needs to be targeted
- If pre-existing hardware (e.g., pedicle screws) exists at the neurotomy site, avoid direct contact with the fusion device

### Sedation Considerations (IPSIS)

- Mild sedation may be used but is **not required** for RFN at any spinal level
- Oral pre-procedure sedatives or anxiolytics may be given as needed
- If moderate sedation is used, the patient **must remain conscious and conversant** to report any unexpected or adverse sensations immediately
- If sedation renders the patient unresponsive, thermal lesioning should be delayed until consciousness is regained

### Motor Stimulation Testing (IPSIS)

- Although recently recommended by a multispecialty working group, **no study has demonstrated that motor stimulation can prevent inadvertent spinal nerve injury during RFN**
- Human and animal studies indicate motor stimulation lacks sufficient sensitivity to prevent thermal injury from an improperly placed cannula
- However, it may be useful at the physician's discretion when anatomic variations or degenerative/surgical changes result in suboptimal imaging
- A previously performed MBB may impair the accuracy of motor stimulation testing
- Sensory stimulation does NOT ensure proper parallel cannula placement and does NOT prevent false-negative results
keyPoints: Patient selection is THE most critical determinant of RFA success
>80% relief on dual controlled blocks is the standard threshold — 50% threshold yields worse outcomes
The JAMA MINT trial (Juch 2017) was heavily criticized for poor patient selection methodology
Medial branch nerves regenerate in 6-18 months; repeat RFA typically needed at 9-18 months
~80% of patients who responded to first RFA will respond to repeat procedures
Do not pursue RFA in young patients (<35) without clear facet arthropathy
Untreated psychological comorbidities predict poor RFA outcomes
Pre-procedure imaging screens for unsafe anatomy (e.g., aberrant vertebral artery) but is NOT diagnostic for facet pain (IPSIS)
Motor stimulation has not been proven to prevent nerve injury during RFN — precise fluoroscopic imaging remains the safety standard (IPSIS)
Patients with PPMs/ICDs need coordinated care with cardiology; continuous ECG monitoring during RFN; dispersive pad >15 cm from leads (IPSIS)
Sedation is not required — patient must remain conversant to report adverse sensations during lesioning (IPSIS)
Adjacent to a posterolateral fusion, the fused-level medial branch is already surgically destroyed (IPSIS)

sections.title: Evidence & Guidelines
sections.content:
## Key Randomized Controlled Trials

### Dreyfuss P et al. (2000) — Spine

One of the most-cited RFA studies, establishing the benchmark for properly selected patients:
- Prospective trial of lumbar medial branch neurotomy in patients selected by **controlled diagnostic blocks**
- **60% of patients achieved at least 90% pain relief at 12 months**
- Significant improvements in physical functioning, lifting capacity, return to work, and medication reduction
- Multifidus EMG confirmed 90% accuracy in nerve ablation
- Success rate of almost 90% for >50% relief for at least one year

### Van Kleef M et al. (1999) — Spine

One of the first high-quality RCTs supporting RFA:
- RCT comparing lumbar facet RFA to sham
- Demonstrated **statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement** in the RFA group at 3, 6, and 12 months
- Established RFA as a legitimate evidence-based intervention

### Nath S et al. (2008) — Pain

Rigorous RCT with **triple blocks** for patient selection:
- Showed significant benefit of RFA over sham for lumbar facet pain
- The strict patient selection (triple blocks) contributed to strong outcomes
- Supports the principle that more rigorous selection yields better results

### Juch JNS et al. (2017) — JAMA (MINT Trial)

Controversial RCT that found no difference between RFA + exercise vs exercise alone:
- **Methodological criticisms**: Single blocks, 50% threshold, 3-month follow-up, technical concerns
- This study is used as a cautionary tale about the importance of patient selection in clinical trials
- Does NOT disprove RFA efficacy in properly selected patients

## Functional Outcomes Data

Dreyfuss et al. (2000) demonstrated improvements across multiple domains:
- **Physical functioning** scores improved significantly
- **Lifting capacity** increased
- **Return to work** rates improved
- **Analgesic medication** use decreased
- **ODI, Roland-Morris, and SF-36** all showed improvement

## Repeat RFA Evidence

- **Rambaransingh B et al. (2010)**: Repeat RFA provides comparable relief to the initial procedure in the majority of patients
- **Son JH et al.**: Demonstrated reproducible outcomes with repeat RFA

## Systematic Reviews

- **Manchikanti L et al.** — Pain Physician: Multiple systematic reviews establishing **Level II evidence** for lumbar and cervical medial branch RFA with controlled diagnostic block selection
- **Lee CH et al. (2017)**: Meta-analysis of RCTs showing significant benefit of RFA over sham

## Duration of Relief

- **Typical duration**: 6-12 months (median ~10 months)
- **Range**: Some patients get 18+ months; others recur at 6 months
- Nerve regeneration via Wallerian degeneration is the mechanism of recurrence

## IPSIS Technical Manual Contributions (2024)

### Cervical RFN Evidence

- The IPSIS technique is built on the original work of Lord et al. (1996, NEJM) and MacVicar et al. (2012) in New Zealand, which used dual MBBs for patient selection, large-gauge parallel cannulae, and multiple lesions
- Recent consensus guidelines (Hurley et al., 2022) provide multispecialty international recommendations for cervical facet interventions
- The IPSIS manual advocates for conventional single large-gauge cannula technique over unvalidated alternatives (cooled RF, bipolar, multi-tined) in the cervical spine until further safety data are available

### Lumbar RFN Evidence

- LMBRFN efficacy is established through the Dreyfuss (2000) and MacVicar (2013, New Zealand) prospective trials using rigorous selection and technical standards
- Schneider et al. (2020) systematic review stratified outcomes by diagnostic methods and procedural technique, showing that rigorous selection and parallel large-gauge electrode placement yield the best results
- The IPSIS technique emphasizes that creating large RF lesions with properly positioned large-gauge cannulae is required for consistent outcomes

### Thoracic RFN — Limited and Evolving

- IPSIS notes that thoracic medial branch RFN is in a period of uncertainty due to recent anatomic findings showing that articular branches may arise proximal to traditional targeting zones
- Despite these concerns, if thoracic MBBs using the traditional technique achieve 80-100% relief, it is reasonable to proceed with RFN at the same target
- Some practitioners supplement thermal RFN with chemical neurolysis in the thoracic spine

### Dispersive Pad Safety

- In a conscious patient with proper dispersive pad placement, skin burn risk is minimal
- The pad must be fully adhered to the skin with its long axis facing the active electrode and placed as far from the electrode as possible
- Higher risk for pad burns exists with higher energy use, longer procedures, sedated patients, and higher BMI patients
keyPoints: Dreyfuss (2000): 60% achieved >90% relief at 12 months with controlled block selection; 90% had >50% relief
Van Kleef (1999): First high-quality landmark RCT showing significant RFA benefit over sham
Nath (2008): Triple block selection yielded strong RFA outcomes over sham
Juch MINT (2017): Negative trial attributed to poor methodology — does NOT disprove RFA in properly selected patients
Repeat RFA provides comparable relief to initial procedure (Rambaransingh 2010)
Level II evidence per ASIPP systematic reviews for RFA with controlled block selection
Typical relief duration is 6-12 months with median around 10 months
IPSIS advocates conventional single large-gauge cannula RFN in the cervical spine over unvalidated alternatives until safety data exist
Schneider (2020) systematic review: best outcomes when stratified by rigorous diagnostic methods AND parallel large-gauge technique
Thoracic RFN is evolving — recent anatomy questions traditional targeting, but positive MBBs still justify proceeding (IPSIS)
Dispersive pad placement: long axis facing electrode, as far from electrode as possible, fully adhered to skin (IPSIS)

sections.title: UpToDate: RFA Evidence by Etiology, Repeat Criteria & Complications
sections.content:
## UpToDate Evidence for RFA Organized by Pain Etiology

UpToDate provides a uniquely helpful framework by organizing the RFA evidence according to the underlying etiology of the patient's pain. This etiology-specific approach is critical for fellowship training because it clarifies that the strength of evidence and expected outcomes vary substantially depending on what structure is being treated.

### 1. Facet Joint Pain — Modest Short-Term Benefit

Small clinical trials evaluating RFA for lumbar facet joint pain have shown either no benefit or modest intermediate-term improvement (less than 12 months), with considerable variation in patient selection criteria and procedural technique limiting generalizability. A 2015 meta-analysis including 23 randomized trials found that radiofrequency denervation modestly reduced short-term pain compared with placebo (mean difference -1.47 on a 10-point scale, 95% CI -2.28 to -0.67; three trials; low- to moderate-quality evidence) but did not improve long-term pain or function. Most included trials were of low or very low quality with limited follow-up. This evidence context explains why patient selection rigor (dual blocks with 80% threshold) is so critical — the trials with the best outcomes are those that used the most stringent selection criteria.

### 2. Discogenic Pain — RFA of the Ramus Communicans (Limited Evidence)

For discogenic pain, RFA targeting the ramus communicans nerve has shown some preliminary evidence of benefit. In one randomized trial of 49 patients with chronic low back pain at a single vertebral level, ramus communicans RFA produced modest improvements in pain and physical function compared with lidocaine injection alone. However, larger studies with more refined patient selection criteria and longer follow-up are still needed before this can be considered a well-established intervention.

### 3. Sacroiliac Joint Pain — Cooled RFA Evidence

RFA has demonstrated benefit for sacroiliac joint pain, particularly using cooled radiofrequency technology in patients who responded positively to a prognostic sacral lateral branch block. In a small randomized trial, cooled RFA of the primary dorsal rami and sacral lateral branch nerves (L4-S3) produced 50% improvement in pain scores compared with placebo at 6-month follow-up. A larger multicenter randomized trial of 210 patients with SI joint pain (diagnosed by positive response to injection) demonstrated that cooled RFA produced modestly improved pain, disability, and quality-of-life scores compared with standard medical management (pharmacotherapy, injections, and integrative therapies) through 12-month follow-up.

### 4. Vertebrogenic Pain — Basivertebral Nerve (BVN) Ablation (SMART Trial Data)

The strongest emerging RFA evidence comes from trials of intraosseous basivertebral nerve ablation in patients with Modic type 1 or 2 endplate changes. In the SMART trial (225 patients with chronic LBP and Modic changes), BVN ablation produced a 20.5-point decrease in average ODI score compared with a 15.2-point decrease in the sham group at three months. Although this difference did not meet the study's prespecified threshold for clinical significance, a subgroup responder analysis found that 75.6% of patients receiving BVN ablation achieved the minimum clinically important difference (MCID) of greater than 10-point ODI improvement, compared with 55.3% of the sham group. In post-study longitudinal follow-up, 76.4% of BVN ablation patients maintained sustained ODI improvement at two years. A subsequent trial of 140 patients was terminated early because the ablation arm uniformly outperformed standard-of-care on all primary and secondary outcome measures. UpToDate notes that non-industry-sponsored studies are still needed to further guide patient selection and quantify effectiveness.

## Repeat RFA: Criteria and Success Rates

While RFA destroys the target nerves, regeneration occurs over time, requiring repeat treatment for sustained benefit. UpToDate provides specific guidance on repeat ablation:
- **Frequency**: Guidelines recommend repeating the procedure no more than two times per year (maximum 2x/year)
- **Success of repeat procedures**: In published studies, repeat medial branch RFA was successful in 60-90% of patients for whom the initial RFA had improved pain symptoms
- **Timing**: Repeat RFA is performed when pain recurs after a previously successful procedure, typically at 6-18 months depending on the pace of nerve regeneration

## Adverse Events: Specific Complication Rates

UpToDate provides specific adverse event rates from clinical trials that are important for informed consent and training:

| Complication | Incidence |
|---|---|
| Transient neuritis (increased pain, lower limb numbness/paresthesias) | 5-10% |
| New-onset radiculopathy | <1% |
| Superficial skin burns | <1% |
| Compression fractures (specific to basivertebral nerve ablation) | Reported but rare |

The neuritis rate of 5-10% is clinically significant and should be discussed with patients during pre-procedure counseling. Patients should understand that temporary worsening of pain for 1-4 weeks after the procedure is a recognized complication related to nerve degeneration, not a sign of procedural failure.

## RFA Not Effective for Radicular Pain

An important UpToDate distinction: conventional (heat) RFA has not been effective for chronic low back pain with radicular symptoms. RFA should not be used for radicular pain — it is reserved for nonradicular etiologies (facet, discogenic, SI joint, vertebrogenic). Pulsed radiofrequency of the dorsal root ganglion is an alternative for refractory radicular symptoms.
keyPoints: FACET RFA: 2015 meta-analysis (23 RCTs) showed modest short-term pain reduction (MD -1.47 on 10-point scale) but no long-term pain or function improvement — most trials were low quality (UpToDate)
DISCOGENIC RFA: Ramus communicans ablation showed modest benefit in one RCT of 49 patients, but larger studies with refined selection criteria are still needed (UpToDate)
SI JOINT RFA: Multicenter RCT of 210 patients showed cooled RFA modestly improved pain, disability, and quality of life through 12 months vs standard medical management (UpToDate)
VERTEBROGENIC/BVN RFA (SMART Trial): 20.5-point ODI decrease vs 15.2-point sham decrease; 75.6% achieved MCID vs 55.3% sham; 76.4% sustained improvement at 2 years (UpToDate)
A second BVN trial of 140 patients was terminated early because ablation uniformly outperformed standard care on all endpoints (UpToDate)
Repeat RFA: maximum 2x/year per guidelines; 60-90% success rate on repeat procedures in patients who responded to initial RFA (UpToDate)
Adverse events: neuritis 5-10%, new radiculopathy <1%, superficial burns <1%, compression fractures reported with BVN ablation (UpToDate)
Conventional RFA is NOT effective for radicular pain — reserved for nonradicular etiologies only (UpToDate)
Non-industry-sponsored studies are still needed for BVN ablation to guide patient selection and quantify effectiveness (UpToDate)

sections.title: Clinical Pearls (Dr. O'Brien)
sections.content:
## Dr. O'Brien on RFA

### It Is a Minor Surgery That Works

Dr. O'Brien considers RFA one of the few back procedures that is actually considered a minor surgery with double-blind randomized trial evidence supporting it. When patients are highly well-selected through dual medial branch blocks with greater than 80% relief, the success rate is remarkable. In the Dreyfuss trial, almost 90% of patients achieved greater than 50% relief for at least a year, and 60% achieved greater than 90% relief.

### Patient Selection Is Everything

Dr. O'Brien's approach to patient selection starts with age and clinical suspicion. He does not pursue RFA in young patients with pristine imaging — he has seen too many 20-year-olds put through medial branch blocks and RFA for nonspecific back pain. The question he asks is: what are you going to do, RFA every six months for the next 30 years?

Instead, he reserves the workup for patients who fit the clinical profile: chronic axial pain, typically one side worse than the other, especially in patients over 50 where disc collapse increases facet joint loading.

### The Dreyfuss Protocol

Dr. O'Brien references Paul Dreyfuss frequently in his teaching. Dreyfuss is a physiatrist who did one of the early prospective trials using dual medial branch blocks with greater than 80% relief threshold. The study used multifidus EMG to verify that the ablation was accurate — and they achieved 90% accuracy in killing the medial branch. This level of rigor in both patient selection and technique verification set the standard for the field.

### RFA Does Not Impair Function

A common concern from therapists and patients is whether denervating the multifidus muscles will impair lifting or spinal stability. Dr. O'Brien points to the Dreyfuss data showing no change in lifting scores pre- and post-RFA. In reality, patients with significant facet pain are not lifting or being active anyway. By reducing their pain, RFA actually enables them to exercise more and become more active.

### The Procedure Is Well-Tolerated

Dr. O'Brien performs RFA without sedation in the vast majority of cases, using 25-gauge needles with local lidocaine. In over 30 years of practice, perhaps five patients in his entire career truly needed IV sedation — those with extreme anxiety or movement disorders. For the rest, the procedure is not that traumatic. This is also the Medicare position: sedation is rarely indicated for these procedures and requires specific medical necessity documentation.
keyPoints: RFA is one of the few back procedures with double-blind RCT evidence supporting its efficacy
Do not perform RFA in young patients with pristine imaging — ask what the 30-year plan is
Dreyfuss protocol: dual MBBs with >80% relief threshold and multifidus EMG verification achieved 90% accuracy
RFA does not impair lifting or function — patients with facet pain are already limited by pain
The vast majority of patients tolerate RFA without sedation using local anesthesia
Patient selection is everything — the rigor of diagnostic blocks directly predicts RFA outcomes
Chronic axial pain, one side worse, age >50 with disc collapse — this is the clinical profile for facet workup
IPSIS RFN supplies: large-gauge (16 or 18G) RF cannulae with 10 mm sharp bent active tip, in 100 and 145 mm lengths; matched electrodes; 25-30G needles for track/MBB anesthesia
Patient comfort can be significantly improved by performing a preliminary MBB and injecting local anesthetic along the cannula track before lesioning (IPSIS)
Stop lesioning immediately if the patient reports adverse sensations — check cannula position in all views before continuing (IPSIS)
For cervical RFN, shoulder traction may improve visualization of C6 and C7 targets — but apply it BEFORE cannula placement as traction after placement may displace the cannula (IPSIS)
